c.tagline: Gateway to the thundering Iguaçu Falls and the tri-border of three nations.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered within the city; agree a price in advance for cross-border trips and airport transfers. Apps like Uber and 99 are common and usually cheaper.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the police (Polícia Militar), 192 the SAMU ambulance service, and 193 the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Caution near the border/Friendship Bridge to Ciudad del Este

hood_desc: Foz's downtown around Avenida Brasil, packed with shops, budget hotels, restaurants and the bus hub; the most central and convenient base for reaching the falls, the dam and the border crossings.
An upmarket residential neighbourhood of quiet tree-lined streets, good restaurants and comfortable hotels, popular with visitors who want a calmer, safer base close to the centre.
The resort corridor along the highway toward Iguaçu National Park, home to the big convention resorts and the park-gate hotels closest to the Brazilian side of the falls.
A well-planned district originally built for Itaipu Dam workers, with wide streets, parks and a settled residential feel close to the dam and northern attractions.
A large commercial-residential district near the Friendship Bridge, with markets, shops and everyday services; handy for shopping trips across to Ciudad del Este in Paraguay.
lodging: Che Lagarto Hostel Foz do Iguaçu

water.note: Tap is treated, but bottled water is widely preferred.

sys.n: Foz do Iguaçu integrated city bus network

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00 AM to midnight, with reduced frequency at night and on Sundays.
transit.pay: Pay the flat fare in cash to the onboard conductor or with the local transit card; the integrated fare at the TTU hub lets you transfer between routes for free.
transit.note: There is no metro or rail. Four private companies run an integrated bus network centred on the TTU (Terminal de Transporte Urbano). Airport and Iguaçu National Park lines run from the TTU, but cross-border routes to Argentina and Paraguay are separate and cost more.

bus: Integrated city buses via the TTU urban terminal
Rodoviária (long-distance bus terminal) for intercity & international coaches

transit.m: City bus line 120 (Aeroporto/Parque Nacional) to downtown via the TTU (~40 min)

tip.r: A 10% service charge is usually added at restaurants; extra tipping is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Churrasco and rodizio
food.desc: Skewers of picanha, ribs and sausage carved at the table until you turn the token red, with a salad and hot-dish buffet alongside.

places.name: Churrascaria Bufalo Branco
places.note: Long-running full rodizio with noble cuts; a Foz standard for big appetites.

places.name: Rafain Churrascaria Show
places.note: Rodizio paired with a Latin American music and dance show; popular with groups.

places.name: Churrascaria Premium
places.note: Central churrascaria with daily buffet, meat rodizio and dessert table.

food.name: Peixe do rio
food.desc: River fish from the Parana basin - surubim, dourado and pacu - grilled or stewed; the local Pira de Foz uses catfish with ginger and cassava puree.

places.name: Terramar
places.note: The city's fish churrascaria, with a grilled-fish rodizio Wednesday to Saturday.

places.name: Tempero da Bahia
places.note: Fish and seafood specialist with moquecas and river-fish plates in a homely room.

places.name: Restaurante Zaragoza
places.note: Long-established Spanish kitchen known for paella and well-handled river fish.

food.name: Chipa
food.desc: Paraguayan cassava-and-cheese bread rings, chewy and warm, sold from baskets and street carts all over the triple-border region.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Foz
places.note: Bakery counters and stalls turn out chipa fresh through the morning.

places.name: Avenida Brasil vendors
places.note: Street sellers work the main shopping avenue with insulated baskets of hot chipa.

places.name: Feira do Produtor
places.note: Producers market where Paraguayan bakers sell chipa alongside cassava and cheese.

food.name: Sopa paraguaia and chipa guasu
food.desc: Border staples despite the name: sopa paraguaia is a dense cornbread with cheese and onion, chipa guasu a softer fresh-corn version.

places.name: Feira do Produtor
places.note: Paraguayan cooks sell trays cut into squares, best bought still warm.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Foz
places.note: Reliable stalls for cornbreads plus mbeju and other Guarani-rooted snacks.

places.name: Ciudad del Este market
places.note: Cross the Friendship Bridge for the same breads at Paraguayan prices.

food.name: Feijoada
food.desc: Brazil's black bean and pork stew with rice, farofa, collard greens and orange slices; traditionally a long Saturday lunch.

places.name: Churrascaria Premium
places.note: Buffet regularly includes feijoada alongside the meat rodizio.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Foz
places.note: Market lunch counters serve the weekend feijoada to local workers.

places.name: Churrascaria Bufalo Branco
places.note: Hot-dish section of the buffet covers feijoada and other Brazilian staples.

food.name: Acai na tigela
food.desc: Frozen Amazonian acai pulp whipped to a sorbet and served in a bowl with granola, banana and honey; eaten as a cooling snack in the heat.

places.name: Avenida Jorge Schimmelpfeng
places.note: Nightlife strip lined with acai and juice bars open late into the evening.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Foz
places.note: Juice counters blend acai bowls to order with tropical fruit toppings.

places.name: Feira do Produtor
places.note: Fruit stalls sell acai pulp and made-up bowls at market prices.

food.name: Terere
food.desc: Ice-cold yerba mate infused with crushed medicinal herbs and drunk through a metal straw from a shared guampa; the border's social ritual.

places.name: Feira do Produtor
places.note: Herb sellers grind the poha nana mixes that go into a proper terere.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Foz
places.note: Buy guampas, bombillas and yerba from stalls that supply local drinkers.

places.name: Praca da Paz
places.note: Public square where locals share terere flasks through the hot afternoons.

food.name: Caipirinha
food.desc: Cachaca muddled with lime and sugar over ice; on the border you will also find versions with maracuja, cashew fruit or caju amazonico.

places.name: Capitao Bar
places.note: Foz institution on the main bar strip, busy every night with live music.

places.name: Rafain Churrascaria Show
places.note: Caipirinhas served through the dinner show; easy for first-timers.

places.name: Avenida Jorge Schimmelpfeng bars
places.note: A whole street of open-air bars mixing caipirinhas until late.

landmarks: Iguaçu Falls (Brazilian Side, Parque Nacional do Iguaçu)
The panoramic trail facing 275 cataracts thundering along a three-kilometer cliff, culminating in a catwalk drenched by the Devil's Throat spray.
Garganta del Diablo (Argentine Side)
The falls' terrifying centerpiece across the border, a U-shaped cauldron where half the Iguazu River plunges 80 meters in a permanent roar.
Parque das Aves
A lush Atlantic Forest bird park beside the falls, where walk-through aviaries bring toucans, scarlet macaws and flamingos within arm's reach.
Itaipu Dam
One of the world's mightiest hydroelectric plants, a binational engineering colossus offering panoramic tours and spectacular nighttime illumination.
Marco das Três Fronteiras
The landmark obelisk where Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet at the Iguazu-Paraná confluence, celebrated with evening folklore shows.
Templo Budista Chen Tien
A serene hillside Buddhist temple with over 120 statues, including a seven-meter Buddha gazing toward Paraguay across the river.
Mesquita Omar Ibn Al-Khattab
An elegant white mosque serving one of Brazil's largest Arab communities, its dome and twin minarets open to respectful visitors.
Macuco Safari
The falls' adrenaline classic, a jungle-trail ride and speedboat charge straight into the crashing spray beneath the cataracts.
Refúgio Biológico Bela Vista
Itaipu's wildlife sanctuary and breeding center, where guided trails introduce rescued jaguars, harpy eagles and native Atlantic Forest flora.
Catedral São João Batista
The city's modernist cathedral, whose sweeping curved roof and stained glass provide a calm counterpoint to the region's natural drama.

train.note: No railway serves Foz do Iguaçu, and Brazil has no intercity passenger trains. The nearest passenger rail anywhere in the region is the Posadas-Encarnación shuttle on the Argentina-Paraguay border, several hundred kilometres south. Arrive by coach or fly into Foz or Puerto Iguazú.

intl.to: Ciudad del Este (Paraguay) - across the Friendship Bridge
intl.op: Transbalan / RTC city cross-border buses — tickets on board

intl.to: Puerto Iguazú (Argentina) - across the Tancredo Neves bridge
intl.op: Río Uruguay / Crucero del Norte — tickets on board or at the Rodoviária

bus.note: This is a genuine tri-border town and the cross-border buses are ordinary city services rather than long-distance coaches - they run every 15-30 minutes from the urban terminal (TTU) and cost very little. Note that they do not always wait while you clear immigration, so if you need an exit or entry stamp tell the driver and be ready to catch the next bus. Long-distance domestic coaches to São Paulo (about 15 hours) and Curitiba leave from the Rodoviária north of town; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/).

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry. The Paraná and Iguaçu rivers here are dominated by the Itaipu dam and the falls themselves, and the boat trips beneath the cataracts are adventure excursions rather than transport. Both international crossings are made by road bridge.
